items.title: Bezzecchi on pole, Marquez claims MotoGP qualifying title
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Aprilia MotoGP rider Marco Bezzecchi took a commanding pole position for the season finale in Valencia, but the retiring Marc Marquez took the 2026 qualifying title.

MotoGP's qualifying championship BMW M Award scores riders by qualifying position using the same top-15 points system as for grand prix finishes, and awards a BMW car to the winner each year.

Marquez was the winner seven consecutive times between 2013 and 2019, and then prevailed in 2025 before doubling up in what has now turned out to be his final season.

Bezzecchi was the only rival who had a shot at denying him a ninth Award in the final round, but second place for Marquez was enough to keep him ahead in the standings - despite the gargantuan 0.463s gap between them.

This came as Bezzecchi obliterated the MotoGP lap record at the track with a searing 1m27.844s.

Raul Fernandez used three soft rear tyres in Q2 and briefly sat on provisional pole but ultimately ended up nearly six tenths behind Bezzecchi in third.

Alex Marquez, Jorge Martin and Fabio Di Giannantonio made it a top six made up entirely of Aprilia and Ducati riders.

Pedro Acosta was third of three KTM riders in Q2, beaten by Enea Bastianini (seventh), stand-in Pol Espargaro (eighth) and also potential 2027 Ducati team-mate Fermin Aldeguer (ninth).

This was despite Espargaro crashing at Turn 1 late on shortly after setting his fastest lap (which he'd spent half of in Acosta's tow).

Ai Ogura, who tumbled at Turn 11 at the end, and Joan Mir completed the Q2 order.

Brad Binder was 0.029s away from a farewell Q2 appearance, losing out to Mir for the final Q1 transfer spot and settling for 13th on the grid - which means team-mate Acosta has maintained a perfect qualifying record versus his team-mates over the first three seasons of his MotoGP career.

Ducati factory stand-in Iker Lecuona was 14th, just half a tenth off Q2, while Johann Zarco was likewise close in 15th - and compatriot Fabio Quartararo led the Yamaha contingent one spot lower.

items.title: Pedrosa leaves KTM MotoGP project
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
KTM's long-serving test rider Dani Pedrosa has exited his role.

The now-41-year-old had joined KTM back in 2018 at the conclusion of his storied career in full-time grand prix racing competition.

He was a marquee signing for KTM, well-regarded for his feedback and feel but also specifically in being lured away from arch-rival manufacturer Honda.

Some notably competitive wildcard outings followed for Pedrosa on the KTM, and he also helped refine a KTM RC16 that at one point had the reputation of being perhaps MotoGP's most recalcitrant machine.

But eventually Pedrosa stepped away from wildcards entirely and also stepped into more of a secondary tester role, emphasising work on rideability while new tester Pol Espargaro became the focal point for performance work.

And with KTM's new 850cc bike for the 2027 regulations now being readied for its debut, Pedrosa - who has also earned acclaim as a TV pundit for Spanish broadcaster DAZN - is ceasing his participation in the KTM project.

KTM motorsport boss Pit Beirer said KTM "can only thank" Pedrosa "for his expertise and passion" and that he "helped us make big steps forward for the project".

"His work with the likes of Mika [Kallio] and Pol and the whole test team pushed us to be where we are today, and his talent was always obvious: we could see this from the times he excited us with his wildcards."

items.title: Hankook's bid for F1 tyre supply - what you need to know
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Hankook has begun a Formula 1 tyre testing programme and opened talks with teams as it prepares to bid on becoming grand prix racing’s official supplier from 2029, The Race has learned.

F1’s current contract with Pirelli runs until the end of 2028, after the Italian company won F1’s most recent tender deal, which covered the period from 2025-2027, against a rival bid from Bridgestone. 

Its contract was extended by a further season in June this year after an option was taken up by the FIA.

From 2029, however, a new tender process is set to be launched by the FIA and there looks set to be fresh competition to secure the right to be the official F1 supplier.

It is understood that Pirelli wants to wait to see details of the tender before deciding if it enters the fray to extend its current spell which stretches back to 2011, while Bridgestone has long evaluated an F1 return with representatives having attended races.

However, it has now emerged that Hankook is ready to throw its hat into the ring too and has been secretly ramping up its own efforts.

Representatives of the company were spotted at the recent Las Vegas Grand Prix, which was understood to have been their second visit to an F1 race this year following a trip to Madrid in September.

The Race understands that Hankook has used these trips to meet a majority of teams and discuss plans with bosses, CEOs and other senior executives.

The trips to races, which also included visits to events in China, Japan and Singapore in 2025, are only one side of its efforts to get ready for 2029, however.

It is understood that Hankook has already committed a 44-person task force within the company to prepare for an F1 entry.

Beyond committing research and development capability plus simulator running, it has this year completed two development tests for F1 rubber using a modified F2-equivalent-mule car to evaluate potential construction as well as different compounds.

A third test has been scheduled to work on its wet-weather rubber, which it hopes can also help it develop a tyre that features a narrower spray plume to reduce visibility problems caused in wet conditions.

Hankook is also working hard on production and manufacturing planning that would be required to supply F1, F2 and F3 tyres that would come under the umbrella of any tyre tender contract.

Hankook is certainly no stranger to FIA competition, with the South Korean company already the official tyre supplier to the World Rally Championship and has just ended its supply to Formula E where Bridgestone is taking over for the upcoming season. Earlier this year Hankook was also named as a global partner of the governing body.

The period of the new F1 tyre tender beyond 2029 will almost certainly cover the transition to the next rules era, with F1 setting sights on new lighter and nimbler cars to coincide with the switch to V8 power units from 2030.

The plans are also set to include a new tyre design, which is set to reduce wheel size slightly from the current 18-inch design.

items.title: Mercedes' early advantage is even scarier than it looks
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Mercedes has been the benchmark 2026 team, but given it’s only won one of the last six races, what’s behind its dominant start to Formula 1’s Qatar Grand Prix weekend? 

World champion Kimi Antonelli led a Mercedes one-two in both practice sessions, four and a half tenths clear of the nearest competition on single-lap pace in FP2 - despite their fastest laps being set on mediums.

Reading into the final classification is a messy endeavour given two red flags disrupted run plans but it actually makes Mercedes’ position even more formidable.

Russell got very close to completing a full lap on softs but did not finish the lap in time - still, his theoretical fastest lap (taking the two sectors he did do on the faster tyre) was some 0.835 seconds faster than the quickest non-Mercedes, Max Verstappen’s Red Bull.

Theoretical best laps FP2 Russell 1m22.683sVerstappen +0.835sPiastri +0.866sHamilton +1.284s

Mercedes’ advantage was also sizeable when looking at the adjusted long-run pace in FP2. You can slice such analysis multiple ways but accounting for laps in traffic as best as possible Antonelli leads the way, a whopping 0.810 seconds faster per lap than Verstappen's Red Bull. 

Antonelli (Mercedes) 1m28.074s

Russell (Mercedes) +0.205s

Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.810s

Hadjar (Red Bull) +1.058s

Norris (McLaren) +1.061s

Piastri (McLaren) +1.173s

*Ferrari didn’t complete a representative long run

Mercedes trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin called it “one of our better Fridays this year” while deputy Mercedes team boss Bradley Lord said Mercedes “hit the ground running” as the car “seems to suit this circuit”.

Lord said there were “very minimal differences” between Antonelli and Russell’s set-ups by the end of the day, with them looking closely matched over both single laps and longer runs. Russell had made some, in his words, “good changes” after FP1 that made him comfortable with the balance. 

Lord said the car is “competitive in both the high speed and the low speed. One of the question marks we had was the low-speed performance with the new update [introduced in Malaysia].

“Obviously, this circuit bias is towards the medium and high speed where we know we've definitely made gains.

“So we're making good use of that. Then hopefully it just reflects our ongoing learning about how to get the most out of the car with this package on it.” 

So there is an element of Qatar playing to the strengths of the package and nullifying the effect of the Malaysia upgrade having put the car in a narrower performance window, for low-speed corners in particular - even if Mercedes has made gains since then in widening it. 

There are far fewer heavy braking zones or tricky corner entries like Mexico, where the W17 struggled more. 

The Mercedes drivers, by and large, avoided the balance issues that have been plaguing rivals like Red Bull in Qatar. 

“They find the key to fix this balance, and this balance issue we can have here by having a massive front limitation in high-speed, medium-speed corners, without compromising the entry,” Red Bull’s technical director Pierre Wache observed. 

“They are able to do that, and we have the work to do to achieve better.” 

Plus, the cars are fairly energy-starved in Qatar - particularly through the high-speed corners and main straight - so the efficiency of Mercedes’ energy management package is rewarded here, as it was in Monza and Baku. 

But the fact it still has a significant advantage over McLaren (with that same power unit) and Red Bull (also with a very strong power unit) suggests it has a lot to do with Mercedes’s strength in high-speed corners and it finding a strong car balance that its rivals can’t. 

Where Red Bull and McLaren are struggling

Max Verstappen has won four of the last six races, but he was struggling with some familiar problems with his RB22.

He suffered team radio issues early in FP1 that were later resolved, but a “disconnected” balance problem remained throughout Friday. 

“It's quite a unique track. It's not an easy track to get things right, so I hope we can do a little bit better,” Verstappen said. 

“The gap to Mercedes is very big, so we need a big jump for that. But I think already from our side, if we can get that balance more together, that's probably already half of the laptime that we're losing.” 

Verstappen also complained of “heavy steering” in FP2 with Wache admitting, “The car is struggling here a lot in terms of kerbing and stuff that will damage. We have to fix that.” 

McLaren’s also wary of the fragility of its car as it started the day on its older specification of floor before switching the drivers onto the new floor introduced in Las Vegas. 

“Many people can run off and damage parts, so we just made sure that we didn't damage any of the new spec for this car,” McLaren’s senior racing director Randy Singh explained. 

McLaren’s power unit exploitation deficit to Mercedes and known baked-in 2026 missteps like short gear ratios explain some of its gap to Mercedes, who Norris said are “just a different level compared to everyone this weekend”. 

“It shows just in general how far off we are. 

“It's not like something works better for them here. I mean, you can just clearly see if they're quick here, they're quick in a lot of other places for the same reason. 

“So I think it's more a realisation of where we stand relative to them.” 

The time loss is most visible on the run to Turn 1, where Norris tops out at 322km/h compared to Antonelli’s 332km/h and has already lost 0.175s by the exit of that corner. 

It’s also present in the high-speed corners at Turn 12-15 where Norris loses another 0.125s, as the more planted Mercedes stretches its legs.  

The Red Bull ends up leaking even more time there as Verstappen loses over three tenths there alone to Antonelli. 

Mercedes has its eye on Red Bull as the “next team”, but Lord said he wouldn’t be surprised to see a five or six-car battle for pole position on Saturday.

There’s clearly one front-running team at risk of being excluded from that fight in Qatar. 

What happened to ‘outlier’ Ferrari? 

The outlier among the top teams on Friday was Ferrari as its drivers didn’t even manage to complete a representative long-run in FP2. Charles Leclerc spun while Lewis Hamilton stopped on-track with a power unit problem. 

“It's been just a very, very difficult session,” Leclerc admitted after FP2. 

“When I lost the car, it probably made it even worse, so we just decided to change the floor, which cost us quite a bit of time. 

“But to be honest, this is not even the reason why we were slow. We were just very slow from the first lap this morning to the last lap in FP2, and it's very difficult to understand what is the outlier. 

“I think not only for us but for everybody, particularly comparing to Mercedes, that seems to be, they always kind of had the best car, but now it's to an extent that we did not expect.” 

As you can see from a comparison of their fastest FP2 laps, Leclerc’s laptime bleed to Antonelli is consistent throughout the lap.

And even on their fastest theoretical laps, there’s major losses in all three of his best sectors - 0.570s in sector one, 0.443s in sector two and 0.484s in sector three. 

That’s likely to lead to a long night of head-scratching from Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren as to why Mercedes appears to be in a different league in Qatar and whether there’s any chance of anyone catching it.

items.title: 100% wear in 15 laps - Qatar tyre issue has got even worse
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Despite the highest front tyre pressures of the season and a maximum stint length already in place, Pirelli is evaluating if further precautions are needed for the Qatar Grand Prix after Friday practice served up “surprise after surprise.”

The Lusail circuit is already the most challenging of the season for tyres, but the evidence from the first day of track running has shown graining, wear and degradation to be at higher levels than anticipated pre-event.

It is suspected this has been caused by a more weathered track surface and the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars that are causing sliding.

On a weekend where there is a much-talked-about 27-lap maximum stint length laid down for each set of tyres, Pirelli has already seen evidence of the most abused front-left sets hitting 100% wear in localised areas after just 15 laps of running on Friday.

Pirelli’s chief engineer Simone Berra said: “It's quite impressive the surprises that this circuit gives to us every time they come here.”

Graining has been encountered on all three compounds - with it particularly aggressive on the C2 and C3. This is accelerating the wear in two specific areas of the tyre - near the inside shoulder and then on the very outside shoulder.

And it is in these specific areas where early analysis has pointed to some wear indicators having hit the 100% level after just 15 laps of high-fuel running in practice.

These elements are also contributing to Qatar producing levels of thermal decay degradation not seen in the past - up to 0.2 seconds per lap - which is going to have an impact on strategies as drivers will not be able to keep pushing on with stints as they have in the past.

On top of all this, Pirelli has also found evidence of gravel cuts in rubber that was returned to it after Friday practice.

Berra said: “We have seen some of them quite deep into the construction. There was also a red flag due to this, and it's something that obviously in a circuit like this, it's an additional variable that can create some attention from our side in terms of punctures.”

Gravel stone cuts discovered after Friday practice last year prompted Pirelli to increase tyre pressures ahead of Saturday running - and a repeat response has not been ruled out right now.

“We are evaluating all the variables,” he said. “If necessary, we will increase the pressure.”

Front pressures are currently at the 29psi set before the weekend, which is the highest they have ever been heading into an event and at the same level Pirelli settled on from Saturday onwards in Qatar last year.

If Pirelli chooses to raise the pressures any more, then they will be the highest they have been in the modern era of F1.

However, Berra is well aware that raising pressures will likely serve to reduce the contact patch of the tyres even more which could potentially increase graining even more.

“That's why I wouldn't increase the pressure if possible,” he said. “But if we have to for integrity reasons, obviously we are going to evaluate it.”

The other action Pirelli is considering in response to the findings about extreme wear of the tyres is reducing the maximum stint length from its current 27 laps.

Berra said that analysis would take place in Pirelli’s laboratory on the tyres used on Friday to see if there are any concerns about their integrity.

“We are going to check them, to section them, and obviously if there is no integrity issue, we will keep the 27 laps in any case because we know that graining level will reduce for the race, and the teams will do much more management to extend the stint length.

“It's an analysis that is ongoing in our laboratory and, with our usual prescription review, we are going to understand if we continue with 27 or not.”

Even if the situation is a marginal one, reducing the stint length may not necessarily be needed because, with degradation in play, Pirelli’s analysis is that it would make no sense for teams to run the maximum distance anyway as it would be too slow.

Instead, with the race distance being 57 laps it is much more logical for teams to split their stints in three equal ones of 19 laps.

However, teams could be forced to shuffle things around based on the timing of safety cars. So even if they headed into the race not intending to run tyres to the maximum distance, they could be tempted to trying to eke out a final 27-lap stint if safety car timing fell that way.

Berra thinks however that the degradation levels seen mean that pace-wise it would not make sense to run for 27 laps - and early safety cars would more likely turn the race into a three-stopper.

items.title: Winners & losers from F1 2026 Qatar GP Friday practice
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Kimi Antonelli led Mercedes team-mate George Russell in both Friday Formula 1 practice sessions for the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix, including an FP2 that was punctuated by two red flags.

Some drivers struggled more than others - and a few lost considerable running over the opening practice sessions - but who are the winners and losers from Friday in Qatar?

Loser: Ferrari (7th & 8th)

If you ask Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton pulling over to the side of the road with a power issue in FP2 was likely the least of Ferrari's worries!

Hamilton was running an older engine for practice, so Leclerc seemed unperturbed by the issue. The bigger problem is that the "pace has just been very, very poor", reckons Leclerc.

"We were just very slow from the first lap this morning to the last lap in FP2 and it's very difficult to understand what is the outlier."

It didn't help that time was wasted changing Leclerc's floor after a spin, but that just distracted from what is Ferrari's real issue. It's slow by any measure and has a big night to try and fix it.

Pirelli’s rubber is taking a battering around the Qatar track - which has sealed its status as the most challenging of the season for tyres.

The Lusail venue delivers graining, high wear, high carcass temperatures because of the fast corners and fatigue risks, plus extra jeopardy caused by gravel stones - and this year things are worse than predicted pre-event.

A combination of the weathered track surface that has got rougher allied to 2026 downforce and performance levels have come together to produce high levels of localised graining that is resulting in some sets reaching 100% wear in localised areas after just 15 laps.

Despite the highest tyre pressures of the season, and a 27-lap maximum stint length for each set having been laid down, Pirelli is conducting analysis tonight to see if even more action needs to be taken ahead of qualifying day to avoid any risk of trouble in the race.

Winner: Mercedes (1st & 2nd)

After two consecutive weekends without a podium finish since wrapping up both its world championships, Mercedes looks in a mega place to end that mini streak here.

It could hardly have hoped for a better Friday. It looks very well balanced, strong in all corner types, and there's a massive one-lap advantage and in the long run too.

Both drivers seem pretty happy with how the car feels, and all of its rivals are worried and feel that Mercedes is in a league of its own.

So this is about as good as any weekend has looked for Mercedes in a long time.

Loser: Red Bull (5th & 6th)

Though Mercedes thinks Red Bull could emerge as its nearest rival come qualifying, right now this is miles off the standard that Red Bull and Max Verstappen have been setting in recent races.

There was a distinct air of unhappiness from the Red Bull camp on Friday evening, with Verstappen bemoaning a car that feels disconnected, a heavy steering problem needing resolving overnight, and just generally Red Bull not looking nearly as sorted with its car balance.

Technical director Pierre Wache is not optimistic that the gap can be closed significantly because it is so big. So this is looking like at the moment Red Bull suffering a chastening Friday that leaves it with lower hopes for the rest of the weekend than its recent mega form would have had it believing in coming into the weekend.

Winner: Racing Bulls (9th & 10th)

You might look at Racing Bulls' performance and think, hmm, leading the midfield as is pretty much usual, nothing to see here.

Peel back the layers and there's quite a lot more going on here.

Its biggest issue is straightline speed, but, as Liam Lawson puts it, that's all "stuff we can see and should be able to fix".

He says the team made a set-up change to an extent that is rarely seen between practice sessions in F1, which team boss Alan Permane confirmed was about adding more rotation into the car with most teams struggling with understeer.

"We already had quite a good car in P1 and now we have an even faster car," reckons Lawson, and the team has a big gap to the next team that only ran the mediums (Audi was closest but on the hards) on long runs.

Loser: Pierre Gasly (10th & 12th)

Gasly’s spin and subsequent beaching cost him valuable time in FP2, the session most representative of qualifying conditions.

The Frenchman said he “should have probably not gone for it” as the tyres were below temperature, he hit the kerbs, and then lost control of the car - damaging the car’s floor in the process.

Furthermore he was “not fully pleased” with the set-up - and Alpine’s managing director Steve Nielsen said the balance is “nowhere near where it needs to be”.

This was never likely to be a great Alpine track given high-speed performance is its biggest weakness but now Gasly is even more on the back foot heading into Saturday.

Winner: Rafael Camara (15th & 17th)

Camara’s trouble-free Friday will come as a relief to the rookie who endured a rocky start to F1 in his home race.

In Qatar, Camara finished ahead of Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman but his long-run pace is of greater importance.

The Brazilian was right on par with Bearman in FP2, under a tenth slower than the Briton over his stint.

It’s looking like the most useful running yet in this cameo ahead of his full-season F1 debut.

Loser: Aston Martin (19th & 20th)

This is looking like a slightly better weekend for Aston Martin than in Las Vegas, but that comes with the extremely big asterisk that it couldn't really be worse.

As it stands, better might just mean not fighting with Cadillac. There are no long runs to be able to judge the team on partly because of the biggest issue of the day, which is that the car didn't seem particularly robust around the challenges of such a parts-breaking circuit.

Aston Martin opted to call it a day with all the disruptions in order to fix what it could, having had a lot of downtime between and during the sessions to try and repair damage.

Mike Krack predicted an evening bonding bits of carbon back together with glue, Lance Stroll has a back problem, and this looks like a tricky start to a weekend that Aston Martin had, in relative terms, slightly higher hopes for.

Loser: Williams (14th & 16th)

Williams hovered around P15 on Friday and neither driver started on the front foot, as both Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon had offs in FP1.

Sainz’s long run was faster than Albon’s on average, but the pair are well behind the rest of the midfield - our analysis putting Williams almost a second behind next-best team Audi and behind Haas.

The Spaniard said he failed to “close” his laps. “There's always snaps, always understeer, there's always a balance that maybe doesn't suit the whole lap and it's difficult to close it.”

That doesn’t bode well for qualifying.

items.title: Antonelli tops Qatar FP2 after multiple red flag delays
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Kimi Antonelli led Mercedes team-mate George Russell again on Friday as two red flags flew in an extended Formula 1 FP2 session in Qatar.

Antonelli set the benchmark of 1m23.077s on medium tyres before a red flag was flown midway through FP2 for gravel and debris from an early spin for Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc.

Shortly after the session resumed, Alpine’s Pierre Gasly beached his car in the gravel to bring out the second red flag. Late on in FP2, the session was extended by 13 minutes.

Russell was 0.127s off his team-mate with neither Mercedes driver improving on soft tyres as they were both interrupted by stoppages. Antonelli had however set the fastest first sector on softs before the second red flags flew.

McLaren pair Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were third and fourth respectively, and around 0.45s off the leading Mercedes. They lined up ahead of Red Bull duo Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar who were half a second off Antonelli’s leading pace.

Half a second behind Hadjar was Leclerc in seventh, with his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton in eighth. Hamilton cut across Verstappen late in the session but the stewards deemed no further investigation was necessary.

The seven-time champion stopped off track with four minutes remaining, triggering a virtual safety car, as his Ferrari lost power.

Racing Bulls completed the top 10 with Liam Lawson ninth and 0.1s ahead of team-mate Arvid Lindblad.

Alpine’s Gasly - whose progress was halted by that trip into the gravel - finished between the Audis of Gabriel Bortoleto in 11th and Nico Hulkenberg in 13th.

Williams' Alex Albon was 14th and team-mate Carlos Sainz was 16th, as they were split by Franco Colapinto in the second Alpine.

Rafael Camara was 17th and ahead of Ollie Bearman as Haas eclipsed the Aston Martins and Cadillac rounded out the standings.

items.title: 50-year-old structure led Williams to F1 cost cap breach
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Williams has explained that overdue company restructuring triggered its Formula 1 cost cap penalty, as it made changes it thought were excluded from the cost cap.

The team was found to have breached the 2025 cost cap by £627,000 (0.48% of the total cap) and will have to pay the FIA a financial penalty - as well as lose 1.5% of its windtunnel and CFD testing time for the next 12 months.

Team boss James Vowles faced a number of questions on the breach during the Friday press conference in Qatar.

“The background to it is that the company structure of Williams was largely unchanged from 1977 and wasn't really fit for purpose in a modern world,” Vowles said.

“We went into it with every intention of being open, transparent with the FIA, which is what we held all the way throughout, but believed those costs, because it's company restructuring, [would] not be a cost cap expense.

“It was the company restructuring that put us over. We’ve had no financial benefit from it, no sporting benefit as a result of it, and you can see that the penalty is pretty much adjusted to be in line with that as well at the same time.

“But it was our interpretation of that, is that those costs are out of cap. The FIA’s interpretation of it are that they are in cap, and obviously we went with the FIA’s interpretation after much discussion.”

Vowles called it a “one-off company restructuring” because the previous structure “wasn't quite fit for purpose”.

Vowles encouraged “those interested” to look at Williams’s accounts on Companies House.

According to Companies House, during 2025 the team “transferred much of its trade and assets to a newly formed subsidiary, Williams Grand Prix Engineering Services LLP, an entity in which the company is a 99% member.

“This update to the corporate structure makes the organisation fit for the future, having been relatively unchanged in the nearly 50 years of operation since formation,

“The changes are about future-proofing our business, enabling smarter ways of working and positioning us to stay competitive at the highest level.

“The inclusion of a partner group will aid retention of certain staff and recognises the importance of those people to the delivery of the business plan.

“Member distributions have been declared to the 1% member of Williams Grand Prix Engineering Services LLP.”

Vowles described it as “Fundamentally, it's a single vertical structure as what was there previously.

“There's many downsides to fundamentally having that. You'll see there's a number of other companies have been created around it, which is just more efficient.

“The costs involved in it are fairly significant. If you think about what you have to do as a business, you probably have, in our case, close to 2,000 contracts with various suppliers and otherwise, that you have to migrate from one company to the next as a result of it. It's a very painful, lengthy task.

“There's some legal that goes with it. There's some compliance you have to do in UK law as a result of it as well at the same time.

“It was a process in the end that took, we initiated it probably around about six months, which probably gives you an idea as to how lengthy it is.

“But it was using finance and legal personnel for that period of which we had to bolster up to get us through that period.”

Williams fell down because it had a different interpretation of the regulations to the FIA.

“Clearly, we should have done something differently as a result of it,” Vowles admitted.

“Although the regulations aren't clear and black and white, it's interpretation, but the FIA is very clear on their perspective, which is the following: Because you've moved contracts from one business to the next, that effectively for them is procurement, which is an included activity.

“For us, we defined it as a financial and legal activity because it's literally taking a contract and changing a name on it.

“I can understand their interpretation, which is why we've accepted the breach, but I hope that helps you understand why it's subtleties, not clarity, really, in that circumstance.”

Vowles isn’t too worried about that 1.5% reduction in windtunnel and CFD testing time given that under the Aerodynamic Testing Restrictions system, there’s a sliding scale of windtunnel and CFD time in 5% increments.

“I think to put things in perspective, one position on the grid is 5% of ATR, and we've got a 1.5% delta. So it's less than a third of a position,” Vowles said.

“I'm rather hoping that we do a better job next year and put ourselves back up the grid, and that would be 15% something in that ballpark.

“So the reality is it's going to be small beans in the grand scheme of things.”

Williams is currently ninth out of 11 teams as of the last ATR period, and that’s unlikely to change for the start of 2027. That table will then reset after the first ATR period ends halfway through 2027 - when by Vowles’s 15% ballpark estimation, Williams will hope to be around sixth in the championship.

items.title: Marquez fastest in his final MotoGP Friday practice session
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Marquez, who stunned the MotoGP paddock by suddenly announcing his retirement at the outset of the day, outpaced '26 title rival Marco Bezzecchi by a quarter of a second with a late burst of speed in the hour-long afternoon session.

He headed an Aprilia 2-3-4, with Bezzecchi narrowly leading the Trackhouse pair of Ai Ogura and Raul Fernandez.

The 0.247s between Marquez in first and Bezzecchi in second was more than the gap between Bezzecchi in second and team-mate Jorge Martin in 10th place, Martin just sneaking into an automatic Q2 spot on Saturday at the expense of former team-mate Johann Zarco (who had a fast crash late on but was unhurt).

Ducati-bound KTM rider Pedro Acosta, who will be expected to spearhead Ducati next year following Marquez's sudden retirement, was fifth (his lap set shadowing Martin), with stand-in Pol Espargaro using Acosta as a reference to place seventh and also secure a Q2 spot.

There were also Q2 spots for Alex Marquez (despite a crash), Fermin Aldeguer and Fabio Di Giannantonio (despite an apparent bike failure).

Both Acosta and KTM stablemate Brad Binder had crashes, Binder ending up well outside the top 10.

items.title: What happened in 2026 F1 Qatar GP first practice
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
New Formula 1 world champion Kimi Antonelli comfortably set the pace in first practice for the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix, despite failing to complete a clean quick lap on the softest tyre compound.

As per usual, medium Pirelli tyres were favoured for the early running in FP1 and Antonelli worked his way down from a 1m25.0s to a 1m24.0s and finally to a 1m23.127s best, which surprisingly stood as the session’s fastest time, regardless of track improvement and everyone using the soft tyre.

Antonelli attempted a soft tyre run of his own but had to abandon the lap after an oversteer moment. He ended the session 0.507s up on Mercedes team-mate George Russell, who found only 0.25s on the softs compared to his best lap on the medium tyre.

Isack Hadjar continued his impressive recent form by setting the third fastest time for Red Bull, ahead of McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who according to Sky F1 both ran with an older specification of floor in this session.

They were separated by just 0.01s and ended the session more than eight tenths off the pace.

Max Verstappen rounded out the top six, 0.916s off, after encountering traffic through the final corner on his best lap.

He also suffered more Red Bull radio problems in this session and complained of needing an impossible 10 more clicks of front wing angle to counter the car’s chronic understeer, while Hadjar lated reported feeling as though his car's front wing wasn't attached such was the lack of front grip.

The Ferraris were well off the pace in seventh and eighth, Charles Leclerc 1.256s slower than Antonelli's benchmark and 0.102s clear of team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls was the quickest of the midfield cars in ninth, a tenth down on Hamilton’s Ferrari and almost three tenths up on Pierre Gasly’s Alpine, which rounded out the top 10.

items.title: Five big revelations from Marquez's retirement announcement
items.author: Eden Hannigan
items.content:
Marc Marquez’s MotoGP retirement announcement was stunning in itself, but the surprises kept coming as he revealed more about his decision timing, how he’d kept the secret and what had prompted it all.

A special press conference was held at Valencia shortly after the weekend’s opening practice session (in which Marquez was narrowly pipped by vanquished 2026 title rival Marco Bezzecchi), with Marquez holding court initially in front of a room packed with the entire grid and scores of team personnel from across the paddock.

He stopped proceedings to arrange a farewell photo with all the rest of the riders, so they could then go and get on with their practice day business.

And then after that, the press conference got under way in earnest.

Here are the key things Marquez revealed.

Marquez opened his account in his exceptional press conference by admitting exactly when and where he had made the decision to retire: at the Japanese Grand Prix at the start of October.

“My decision was done after Motegi,” Marquez revealed, also sharing that “the only person in the world [to] know was my brother Alex.”

Nobody else knew prior to this week about his impending announcement either, as he only told his father, Julia, on Wednesday night, and his mum found out this morning, one hour before the announcement.

Even Ducati was kept in the dark over the news, with Marquez revealing his plans to general manager Gigi Dall’Igna and other key personnel in the factory only set up on Thursday.

Part of the reasoning over the secrecy was his closeness to his brother, but also because of the amount of energy it took to even speak about any kind of retirement.

He was retiring regardless - win or lose

Regardless of the outcome of the championship, Marquez says his mind was made up at Motegi, and that it “[didn’t] matter if I win or if I finish second or third.”

After that weekend, he was two points shy of leader Jorge Martin, and 47 ahead of his Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi.

Ever the pragmatist, Marquez followed his instincts to end his career now, adding that following his instincts has proven statistically smart in the past.

Asked whether retirement had been a discussion before he spoke with his brother in Japan, he said: “No, because this is another thing. In the other times, 2023 was the only time. And I was discussing with my people, because I had doubts, because I felt like, ‘OK, I can do it again’.

“But then we find the way, because in that moment, I need help from my people and my people, when I need help, they are always there.

“But this time I was fully convinced, no discussion. I said to [Alex], it doesn't matter if I win or if I finish second or third. And at that time, the championship was very close.

“But I say, ‘the correct thing, my instincts say, this is the way’. And most of the time in my career, when I follow my instincts, the statistics say that was the good way. So I follow the statistics.

“But this time I'm more than convinced that that is the correct thing for my personal and professional life.”

The injury that scares him most came back

Marquez’s body has been through so many surgeries, even before the career-threatening 2020 injury and its complex, years-long repercussions, and the hugely significant Mandalika 2025 and Le Mans 2026 crashes.

But amid all the many, many broken bones, it’s the bouts of double vision that have really scared him.

And he revealed on Friday for the first time that they’d reoccurred in both his last major injuries and that this had made him worry for his quality of life beyond racing - and take more care for the rest of the season as a result.

“Of course, you can work, of course, you can fight, I'm a fighter, but there's another point that I'm scared, and I start to feel the fear,” said Marquez.

“And it's not the fear of the bikes, it's not the fear of the speed, it's an injury that is there, but at the moment, it's not affecting my personal and professional life.

“After the Indonesian GP [in 2025], as part of my injury on the arm, I had double vision again, only for 48 hours.

“After Le Mans, I had another double vision again, only for 12 hours.

“Luckily, those two times I was able to recover well, and it was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk, and why I crashed less this second part of the season.”

Marquez had his first bout of double vision way back in his Moto2 days, following a heavy practice crash at Sepang in 2011 when he was challenging Stefan Bradl for the title as a rookie.

He was sidelined for four months as a result, and required surgery before he could race again, but it didn’t stop him from returning and dominating Moto2 in 2012 then graduating straight to MotoGP and commencing his extraordinary run of immediate success there.

It didn’t occur again until a training crash at the end of 2021, and then it flared up again very soon afterwards as a consequence of his horrendous Mandalika warm-up crash in early 2022.

Having not happened for 10 years, for it to occur four times in the next five was clearly too disconcerting for Marquez.

Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news.

How he handled racing with this secret

Asked how he’d been able to focus on the five racing weekends he’d done since making his decision, amid the title fight too, Marquez said that was partly because “nobody knows, only Alex”.

That meant he didn’t have to think or talk about it with the wider world.

The other thing that helped him was a message from an unnamed “legend of MotoGP” who gave him the advice to “promise something to your body and your body will give extra”.

From there on, Marquez said he would keep reminding himself that it would be the last time he would race at each of the venues, and that it gave him the extra drive and performance to make it through each weekend.

He also addressed why he looked so “serious” after some of his sprint podiums, notably at Sepang where he seemed disappointed with a second-placed finish behind Pedro Acosta.

It wasn’t because he was angry, “It was because I was suffering,” Marquez said. “I was suffering and the results covered my real situation.”

Making big decisions in life always comes with some semblance of doubt.

But for Marquez, his conclusions were clear - and crucially, made at a time where he was free from the worst of his injury woes.

Asked by The Race whether he had second-guessed his choice at all in the weeks that followed, he said: "No, because as I always say, you cannot take any decision when you are injured or when you are on your peak of adrenaline. And then the decision I made when I was there alone in Twin Ring Motegi, I was quiet.

“And in that weekend, I said, it's the time. Of course, there were some races that I was thinking. But then, yeah, I feel like it was the time, many things on the limit.

“And we are humans. And as I say, I started to feel the fear. It didn't affect me, because then I have the capacity to fully concentrate.

“But just to think about, again, double vision. Of course, in life, you have risk. But if you are competing, you have more risk.

“So in the end, it's trying to understand all your situations, the amount of effort you put in your career, especially the last years, and life continues.

“So this is the most important, and it's something that I understood in 2020 and 2021. Before that, I thought there was no life out of the paddock. There, I understand that life continues.”

Pedro Acosta - whose 2027 at Ducati now looks pretty different - was sixth, while Johann Zarco crashed towards the end of FP1 but still took seventh over Fabio Di Giannantonio. 

Martin was ninth, 0.504s off team-mate Bezzecchi’s best time, as Ai Ogura completed the top 10.

items.title: Ducati's candidates to replace Marquez
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
The shock news that Marc Marquez will call it quits on MotoGP at the end of this weekend creates a massive dilemma for Ducati, as it now tries to figure out exactly how to replace its star rider only days after he clinched another title success for the team and with 2027 testing about to begin.

Not since Jorge Lorenzo dramatically retired at the end of the 2019 season has a factory team had to find a new racer at the final round of the season, but it’s fair to say that the retirement of Marquez will create substantially more ripples through the grand prix paddock than his former rival’s did.

The most obvious solution, of course, is that Ducati promotes one of the rest of its line-up and, given the support and trust that Ducati Corse boss Gigi Dall’Igna has placed in since signing him as a then-rookie on a four-year MotoGP deal, it’s hard to imagine that it would be anyone else right now. That will create a vacancy at the VR46 team Aldeguer is currently scheduled to ride for next season.

Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news.

The only other obvious contender is VR46's other 2027 signing: reigning World Superbike champion and 2027 MotoGP rookie - and the decision between which of the two is likely to get the nod will probably be measured in something that only Ducati has access to: lap times from testing on the 850cc bikes being used next year.

Aldeguer has already had a chance to jump onto next year’s factory bike, deputising for the departing Pecco Bagnaia at two post-race tests, but we’ve not heard much about how he performed in those closed-to-the-media outings at Brno and the Red Bull Ring.

However, while Aldeguer has had his time on the 850, Bulega has essentially been the lead development rider for the project thanks to his WSBK position meaning he’s not held back by MotoGP’s testing restrictions - and the initial suggestions have been that he has been very, very fast indeed.

Either way, though, the promotion of one of them to sit alongside Pedro Acosta in the most coveted seat in MotoGP will leave a space (ironically) at Valentino Rossi’s VR46 satellite team - a seat that might actually be harder to fill than Marquez’s.

The obvious choice, of course is Spanish Moto2 championship contender Manu Gonzalez, who goes into this weekend’s final race with a slender 4.5 point lead over already-confirmed 2027 MotoGP rookie Izan Guevara - and who many feel like has already been overlooked for a premier class seat for the past two seasons.

He already has limited MotoGP experience after standing in for Ai Ogura at Trackhouse Aprilia for a post-race test last year, and he certainly didn’t embarrass himself there. And while he’s already renewed with his IntactGP team for Moto2 next year, most contracts have a MotoGP escape clause - that is, after all, how Alex Marquez ended up joining his brother Marc at Repsol Honda in 2020, when he replaced Lorenzo.

One name that deserves to be in the conversation, of course, is this weekend's second factory Ducati rider , who has completed a number of very impressive MotoGP stand-in rides this year alongside his World Superbike duties.

However, he might have created a cross for his own back with a strong run of form as Bulega's number two this season, with Ducati's production bike hopes now resting firmly on his shoulders for 2027.

Of course, there’s an argument for helping one of the current MotoGP refugees find a spot for next year instead, with race winners such as and without a ride as things stand right now - but that will likely be a question decided on whether Ducati wants to invest in future potential, or is just looking for a one-year seat filler before is can settle things longer term during 2027.

That option might be interesting to the team, though, because it disrupts MotoGP’s two-year contract cycle a little - and potentially even opens the door to Marquez’s protege finding his way onto the MotoGP grid a little earlier than initially expected.

There’s a very short timeline on making those decisions, though, because Ducati will absolutely want its new rider, whoever it is, to make their debut for the factory next Tuesday at the post-race test, so that it can start the process of moulding them into a MotoGP racer sooner rather than later.

items.title: Our verdict on Marc Marquez's bombshell MotoGP retirement
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Marc Marquez dropped a huge bombshell as the final MotoGP round of the season kicked off at Valencia by announcing he is retiring from racing after this weekend.

Here's our take on the decision.

Who can blame him? Going out on top

There have been suggestions for weeks that Marc would retire at the end of the season, but it’s absolutely worth stressing this: almost none of them have come from inside the MotoGP paddock, with nearly everyone that you speak to (including people very much inside the Marquez inner circle) almost certain that he would continue on.

There was, so went the belief, still so much to come. New regulations for next year, and the chance to do what he’s never done and win on a different spec of bike. The opportunity to give us the moment Casey Stoner denied us, and test himself against his hotshot new Ducati team-mate Pedro Acosta.

Instead, he’s walked away - and honestly, after countless surgeries, dozens of broken bones, and 10 world titles, who can blame him? He’s going out on top, on his own terms.

What it says about his 2026 title

My apologies for bringing Formula 1 into this - I will keep it short. I remember being a fresh-faced editorial assistant when Nico Rosberg dropped his retirement announcement on us in 2016, and while those memories are so incredibly distinct (at home versus on track, new to the industry versus much more settled), the vision of it all is surprisingly similar.

When Rosberg got his one F1 title over the line, it was knife-edge. We all knew - he probably knew, too - that this was the one and only. He clearly accepted that quickly and was happy to leave it at that.

Marquez has won eight in MotoGP, but this is the first one he's won in this way. This is the first one that felt truly knife-edge, that felt lost and then found, that felt like it was taking more out of him than ever before and something different out of him than before.

He points-raced to it, with just a handful of crashes from his return at Mugello six months ago to now, whereas normally he was the one leading the crash standings. This time he played the odds and the opponent, and had to convince his body - the much-suffering arm, the diminished shoulder - to play along.

I have little doubt he could have won again. But I genuinely believe he no longer liked the odds, and could no longer justify to himself all the physical travails that would continue to be required to maintain those odds.

This adds to the legacy of his 2026 title, that I for so long didn't believe in. It was such a tightrope act that it's made the greatest rider in MotoGP history go 'OK, that was crazy - crazy enough to call it a day'.

Absolutely the right decision but a huge 2027 loss

Given everything his body has been through, everything he has achieved, this is absolutely the right moment for Marc Marquez to retire. He has nothing more to prove and there is no point risking yet more injuries. Totally, totally the right call.

But I am so, so, so gutted that we will now never get to see how him versus Acosta in the same team would have panned out.

Stoner's shock retirement months before Marquez arrived in MotoGP deprived us of one epic head to head, but was totally the right call for Stoner.

Now Marquez has deprived us of something that would have been even more epic.

But good for him. He's picked his moment perfectly.

The greatest I have ever seen

I'll keep it short and sweet: he has earned this moment. The amount of pain, suffering and ability to keep coming back again and again has finally taken its toll on him.

He retired on his terms, something that he may have thought might not have been possible just a few months ago with the state of his right arm. To win his 1oth world title through sheer mental strength and earn the right to be called the greatest motorcycle rider of all time is the perfect ending.

The greatest I have ever seen, what a pleasure it has been.

Stops any doubt about GOAT status

Marc Marquez's bombshell retirement will cement him as MotoGP's Greatest of All Time.

He was already that in my view - he's beaten many of MotoGP's other GOAT contenders to his first titles, and then won more after completing one of sport's great injury comebacks post-Jerez 2020 (and all the setbacks that followed).

But retiring now on his own terms ensures that nothing that happens in 2027 will change that.

Acosta was the only rider who I felt would have half a chance against Marquez on the same bike, and now Marquez won't be going head-to-head with him.

Had Marquez tripped up there - something not out of the question, given he'd have to adapt to a whole new formula and Acosta's enormous potential - that may have put an asterisk over his status as the GOAT.

Instead, Marquez has left the building and leaves behind a scrap to be MotoGP's new benchmark rider, a fight I wouldn't be surprised if his Ducati successor wins.

From a selfish point of view as an observer and fan of MotoGP, I don't want Marc to stop. But I get why it's happening. The mission is complete.

He's been through hell since 2020, fought back to the top of the mountain, got hurt a few more times along the way, and after dominating 2025 pulled off an unthinkable comeback in 2026.

What else is there left to achieve? How many more times should he risk destroying his body just because his presence in MotoGP is box office?

Of course I'd have loved to see him up against Acosta on equal machinery. But we'll just have to add that to the long list of epic head-to-heads we've narrowly missed out on in many forms of motorsport dating back decades.

Marquez has carried MotoGP on his shoulders for long enough. Those shoulders deserve a break, and now it's time for new stars to lead the series into its Liberty-owned era. Who's going to step up?

I expected to be making a coffee at the start of FP1, not watching the greatest MotoGP rider of all time announcing his retirement on some slides.

Taking a step back, this shouldn’t really be as shocking as it is, and yet we’re all speechless. This is a man whose body has been battered by countless injuries and surgeries over his career, but especially the last six years. This was a championship which came from 102 points back after yet more injury.

He’s now stepping away at the very top of his game, coming back from years of turmoil to reclaim his crown - not just once, but twice.

It is, of course, a shame that we won’t see Marquez vs Acosta, that much awaited battle between the king and the heir.

But whatever happens, it is beyond doubt now that Marc Marquez did it better than anyone else.

Blah blah blah, yeah yeah yeah… but ten.

He's never seemed so physically spent

Friday’s FP1 is usually a lower key ambience to kick off the weekend. But the eerie silence as the camera cut to Marc Marquez let us know something was up.

Ever the maestro of conducting the media off track, it was simple but utterly shocking to read the words 'This will be my last race in MotoGP'.

I expected a playful '…for 2026' to follow on a final card, but no. This is the end - mercifully, on track, on his own terms.

We will not see Marc on the next generation of MotoGP bikes. There will be no Honda reunion and no head to head with Pedro Acosta as Ducati’s newest prince in waiting.

There will not be an 11th world championship title. But for all the tantalising future narratives we lose, what an extraordinary chapter of MotoGP history we have witnessed.

The talent hasn’t diminished, the mind is sharper than ever, but the injuries have now clearly taken a toll too far to continue.

Reflecting on his 2026 season, Marc has never seemed so physically spent after his sessions, so there is a logic to this timing.

The 1000cc chapter closes, he has given everything, leaving this extraordinary sport battled-scarred but having made an impact as one of the true legends of motorcycle racing.

Someone give Gigi Dall’igna a hug, he’s had an emotional 24 hours.

Robs us of tantalising Acosta battle in 2027

In many ways, Marquez’s retirement makes sense: he arguably has nothing more to achieve, his body is already broken enough, and a retirement on his own terms is nothing less than he deserves.

I feel quite sentimental about the end of this chapter though. Hearing Marquez’s story about his attempted comeback in Jerez after that 2020 crash is what got me into MotoGP. Following along with his journey back from all of those injuries and struggles at Honda to his successes with Ducati has been incredible to watch.

He’s also cemented his status as the greatest of all time in my book, especially over the last two season. Could he have won again in 2027? I think so, but that’s something only he knows for sure.

So happy to have witnessed the (tail-end) of a stellar career and happy that he can end it this way. That being said, I’m slightly annoyed that we’ve been robbed of what could have been blockbuster battles between Marquez and Acosta at Ducati in 2027, and also extremely curious about what comes next.

I pity the first 'after-Marc' world champion

I sort of pity the first A.M. (after Marc) MotoGP world champion...

My main disappointment is we won't see if anyone could have properly overthrown him.

He'd so emphatically reminded everybody he was the best in the business that maybe he wouldn't have been beaten, of course. 

It'll just feel slightly hollow for whoever succeeds him as world champion because justifiably or not there'll probably be that little asterisk of 'well, he only won because Marc stopped'. 

I'm trying to consider a hypothetical F1 alternative that fits better than the obvious comparison of Nico Rosberg in 2016. 

Rosberg was world champion but he wasn't the best driver in F1 at the time. So he couldn't be 'dethroned,' but I don't think there was an overarching 'ah, man, it would have been good to see who could have beat him' at play there. 

With Marquez you know that MotoGP's losing the absolute benchmark.
